---
title: "Hurst's H on Indian city rainfall - how big a reservoir?"
output: html_notebook
---

Harold Edwin Hurst spent decades on the Nile working out how big the Aswan
reservoir had to be. His question: if you want to release the long-run average
flow every year, how much water must you store to ride out the runs of dry and
wet years? For a series of independent years the required storage grows like
`sqrt(N)`. Hurst found the Nile grew faster - wet years clump with wet years,
dry with dry - so you need a much bigger dam than randomness would suggest.

He summarised this with the rescaled range. Take annual values, and the
cumulative departure from the mean `Z_t = sum(x_i - xbar)`. The range
`R = max(Z) - min(Z)` is exactly the storage a reservoir needs to guarantee
the mean release over that window (the Rippl mass-curve argument). Divide by the
standard deviation to get `R/S`, and `R/S ~ (a N)^H`. `H = 0.5` is a random
series; `H > 0.5` is persistence. The Nile sits around 0.7.

Two numbers per city here: `H` (the persistence exponent) and, more concretely,
`R / mean` - how many years of average rainfall the reservoir must hold.

```{r}
require(tidyverse)
require(arrow)

ds <- open_dataset("rainfall_parquet")
lookup <- read_parquet("cell_lookup.parquet")
```

Same nine cities as the other notebook, same cell lookup.

```{r}
tribble(
  ~city       , ~pattern                  ,
  "Delhi"     , "^(New )?Delhi$"          ,
  "Mumbai"    , "^Mumbai$"                ,
  "Kolkata"   , "^Kolkata$"               ,
  "Chennai"   , "^Chennai$"               ,
  "Bengaluru" , "^(Bengaluru|Bangalore)$" ,
  "Hyderabad" , "^Hyderabad$"             ,
  "Ahmedabad" , "^Ahmedabad$"             ,
  "Pune"      , "^Pune$"                  ,
  "Jaipur"    , "^Jaipur$"
) -> city_patterns

city_patterns %>%
  mutate(
    cell = map2(city, pattern, function(city, pattern) {
      lookup %>%
        filter(str_detect(name, regex(pattern, ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
        slice_max(population, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
        transmute(city = city, cell_lat, cell_lon)
    })
  ) %>%
  select(cell) %>%
  unnest(cell) -> city_cells

city_cells
```

Annual total per city cell, 1951-2024. Post-1951 only (better gauge coverage),
and drop 2025 - it's provisional and half-formed.

```{r}
ds %>%
  filter(lat %in% city_cells$cell_lat, lon %in% city_cells$cell_lon) %>%
  group_by(lat, lon, year) %>%
  summarise(annual_mm = sum(rainfall_mm), .groups = "drop") %>%
  collect() %>%
  inner_join(city_cells, by = c("lat" = "cell_lat", "lon" = "cell_lon")) %>%
  transmute(
    city = factor(city, levels = city_patterns$city),
    year,
    annual_mm
  ) %>%
  filter(year > 1950, year < 2025) %>%
  arrange(city, year) -> city_yearly

city_yearly %>% summarise(n = n(), .by = city)
```

The core Hurst piece. `rs_range` is the storage number - range of the cumulative
departure from the mean. Everything else is built on it.

```{r}
rs_range <- function(x) {
  z <- cumsum(x - mean(x))
  max(z) - min(z)
}
```

Before any exponent, look at the actual mass curve. This is what Hurst was
staring at. Bengaluru: cumulative departure from its own 1951-2024 mean. The
reservoir has to span the gap between the highest and lowest point of this line.

```{r}
city_yearly %>%
  filter(city == "Bengaluru") %>%
  mutate(cum_dep = cumsum(annual_mm - mean(annual_mm))) -> blr_mass

blr_mass %>%
  summarise(
    top = max(cum_dep),
    bot = min(cum_dep),
    top_yr = year[which.max(cum_dep)],
    bot_yr = year[which.min(cum_dep)]
  ) -> blr_R

blr_mass %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, cum_dep)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +
  geom_line(colour = "#1b7a7a", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = 2028,
    xend = 2028,
    y = blr_R$bot,
    yend = blr_R$top,
    arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.15, "cm")),
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2030,
    y = (blr_R$top + blr_R$bot) / 2,
    label = paste0(
      "R = ",
      scales::comma(round(blr_R$top - blr_R$bot)),
      " mm\n~ ",
      round((blr_R$top - blr_R$bot) / mean(blr_mass$annual_mm), 1),
      " years of\naverage rain"
    ),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.2,
    colour = "grey30",
    lineheight = 0.95
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1951, 2045), clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Bengaluru's rainfall mass curve, and the reservoir it implies",
    subtitle = "Cumulative departure from the 1951-2024 mean; the dam must span top to bottom",
    x = NULL,
    y = "cumulative departure (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(r = 60))
```

Before looking at cumulative departures, compare the annual totals directly.
Each panel has its own horizontal mean line, so the year-to-year variability is
visible without mixing cities with very different rainfall levels.

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
city_yearly %>%
  summarise(mean_mm = mean(annual_mm), .by = city) -> city_means

city_yearly %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, annual_mm)) +
  geom_hline(
    data = city_means,
    aes(yintercept = mean_mm),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    colour = "#b5651d",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = "#1b7a7a", size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~city, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Annual rainfall for the nine cities",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows each city's 1951-2024 mean",
    x = NULL,
    y = "annual rainfall (mm)"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'loess', span = 0.2, linewidth = 0.6, se = F ) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = F, linewidth = 0.3, lty = 2)  +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

Now put the same mass curve beside the others. Each panel is centred on that
city's own 1951-2024 mean, so the vertical span is directly comparable as the
storage range `R` (though the panels use free y-scales so each city's shape stays
readable).

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
city_yearly %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(cum_dep = cumsum(annual_mm - mean(annual_mm))) %>%
  ungroup() -> city_mass

city_mass %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, cum_dep)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey85") +
  geom_line(colour = "#1b7a7a", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~city, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Rainfall mass curves for the nine cities",
    subtitle = "Cumulative departure from each city's 1951-2024 mean; the top-to-bottom span is the implied storage range",
    x = NULL,
    y = "cumulative departure (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

The line drifts up for decades then down - that slow wander is persistence, and
it's why the range is big. A coin-flip series would hug zero.

Now the exponent. Classic R/S: split the series into non-overlapping windows of
length `n`, average `R/S` within each `n`, and regress `log(R/S)` on `log(n)`.
The slope is `H`.

```{r}
hurst_H <- function(x, ns = c(8, 10, 12, 16, 24, 36, 74)) {
  ns <- ns[ns <= length(x)]
  tibble(n = ns) %>%
    mutate(
      rs = map_dbl(n, function(n) {
        k <- length(x) %/% n
        map_dbl(seq_len(k), function(i) {
          seg <- x[((i - 1) * n + 1):(i * n)]
          rs_range(seg) / sd(seg)
        }) %>%
          mean()
      })
    )
}
```

The log-log fit for a few cities, so the slope is visible rather than asserted.

```{r}
c("Bengaluru", "Kolkata", "Ahmedabad") %>%
  set_names() %>%
  map_df(
    function(ct) {
      city_yearly %>% filter(city == ct) %>% pull(annual_mm) %>% hurst_H()
    },
    .id = "city"
  ) -> rs_fits

rs_fits %>%
  ggplot(aes(log(n), log(rs), colour = city)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1b7a7a", "#b5651d", "grey55")) +
  labs(
    title = "Rescaled range grows as a power of window length",
    subtitle = "Slope of each line is that city's Hurst H",
    x = "log(window length in years)",
    y = "log(R/S)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
```

Kolkata's line is steepest (most persistent), Ahmedabad's flattest (closest to a
random series). Now compute both numbers for all nine.

```{r}
city_yearly %>%
  summarise(
    mean_mm = mean(annual_mm),
    R_mm = rs_range(annual_mm),
    store_years = R_mm / mean(annual_mm),
    H = coef(lm(log(rs) ~ log(n), data = hurst_H(annual_mm)))[["log(n)"]],
    .by = city
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(store_years)) -> hurst_tbl

hurst_tbl %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(., 2)))
```

Pune's ~16 years of storage isn't real fractal persistence - that cell carries a
strong monotonic trend over 1951-2024, and raw R/S reads any trend as extreme
persistence (its H of 0.87 sits with the others, but the range is three times
anyone else's). Flag it, don't trust its storage number. Everyone else lands in
a believable band. On the shorter post-1951 record the exponents run high across
the board - Bengaluru and Pune at 0.87, Kolkata 0.85, Delhi 0.83, Mumbai 0.80 -
all well above the Nile's ~0.7, so wet and dry years genuinely clump. Hyderabad
(0.52) and Ahmedabad (0.57) are closest to a memoryless coin-flip series.

The concrete dam number, ranked. How many years of its own average rainfall each
city would have to bank to always release the mean.

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
hurst_tbl %>%
  mutate(city = fct_reorder(city, store_years)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(store_years, city)) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = 0, xend = store_years, yend = city),
    colour = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(size = H), colour = "#1b7a7a") +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = paste0(round(store_years, 1), " yrs  ", "(H=", round(H, 2), ")")
    ),
    hjust = -0.25,
    size = 3.2,
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 6), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.28))) +
  labs(
    title = "Delhi's rainfall would need the deepest reservoir",
    subtitle = "Years of average rainfall to store for guaranteed mean release; dot size = Hurst H. Pune dropped (trend-driven outlier, 15.9 yrs)",
    x = "storage required (years of mean rainfall)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )
```

Higher `H` and higher storage roughly track each other - persistence is what
forces the big reservoir - but not perfectly, because storage also depends on how
far the wet and dry runs actually swing, not just on the correlation structure.
